title: Doughnut-chart Configuration
description: A doughnut/pie chart widget for visualizing proportional data as circular segments. Use this widget to display part-to-whole relationships, such as market share percentages, budget allocations, or the split of a total into a fixed set of parts (good vs scrap, running vs idle time). The slices are a fixed list set in the configuration, each with its own value, so the parts must be known in advance. Supports several doughnuts in one tile, one per dataseries entry or one per distinct value of a pivot column, drawn as separate charts arranged automatically in a grid that uses the tile best (nested rings are not supported), and a configurable hole size (set to 0% for pie chart). Best for 2-8 slices per doughnut where comparing relative proportions is important.

aiSelection.dataShape: A fixed list of named parts written in the config, each with one numeric size: dataseries[].sections[][] holds the slices as {name, value, color?, pivot?} (slices live at sections[][], not sections[], and use `name`, not `label`). The parts are drawn as shares of their common total, so the values must be summable quantities (counts, amounts, durations) rather than rates or averages. When sections is bound with a tableRef, EACH ROW of the result is one whole doughnut: the format is a list with one entry per slice, each `value` a column of that row and `name` usually a `$str:` constant, e.g. [{name: '$str:Good', value: 'good_parts'}, {name: '$str:Scrap', value: 'scrap_parts'}]. Only the NEWEST row is drawn, or with dataseries[].settings.averageLatest = N each slice is the mean of that slice over the newest N rows (matched by position). A slice's value can instead be its own valueRef. The widget never turns rows into slices: data with one row per category (e.g. a GROUP BY cause with summed minutes) draws one 100% slice. Binding the same column to sections[][].pivot on every slice draws one separate doughnut per distinct value; each dataseries[] entry is a doughnut of its own, titled with its label. Reads best with 2-8 slices.
useWhen: The question is what share each of a fixed, known set of parts has of a whole, and each part's size is a column of one row or a value of its own — good vs scrap parts, running / idle / fault minutes already totalled into columns, budget allocation.
The numbers are parts of one total and the proportions matter more than the absolute values.
A pie chart is asked for rather than a doughnut: same widget, set dataseries[].settings.cutout to '0%'.

One doughnut per machine, site or period should be generated from a single column — bind it to sections[][].pivot on every slice (e.g. a Good/Scrap doughnut per machine) — or a few separate breakdowns should sit side by side, one dataseries[] entry each.
notFor: Comparing magnitudes across categories that are not shares of a total, or where there are more than about eight of them — use widget-linechart with dataseries[].type: 'bar'. Bars compare lengths, which the eye judges far better than angles.

Shares whose categories are ROWS of the result — one row per cause, program or machine, such as a GROUP BY cause with summed minutes — or whose categories are not known in advance. The slices are a fixed list written in the config and the widget never turns rows into slices, so such data draws one 100% slice. Use widget-linechart with dataseries[].type: 'bar' and axis.timeseries: false (the category on the x axis), or widget-table when the exact numbers matter.
A quantity changing over time — a doughnut has no time dimension. Use widget-linechart.
Which state something was in over time, and when — use widget-statehistory. Total time per state, once aggregated into columns of one row, can be shown here as shares.
A single figure with no parts — use widget-value, or widget-gauge when it has a meaningful minimum and maximum; a doughnut of one slice is always 100%.
Reading exact numbers rather than proportions — use widget-table, or a bar chart with dataseries[].styling.showValueLabels enabled.

title.title: Title
title.description: The main heading displayed above the doughnut chart. Use to describe what data is being visualized.

subTitle.title: Subtitle
subTitle.description: Secondary text displayed below the title. Use for additional context like time period, data source, or units.

columnLayout.title: Vertical Layout
columnLayout.description: When enabled, the doughnuts are stacked in one column. When disabled or unset, they are arranged automatically in a grid that uses the tile best.

dataseries.title: Doughnuts
dataseries.description: Array of doughnut chart configurations. Each entry draws its own doughnut chart, titled with its label, or one doughnut per distinct value when its slices are split by a pivot column. The doughnuts are separate charts, arranged automatically in a grid that uses the tile best (or stacked in one column with Vertical Layout) in the order of this list; they are never drawn as rings nested inside each other. Use several entries to show different data or perspectives of the same dataset side by side.

label.title: Label
label.description: The title shown above this doughnut. When the slices are split by a pivot column, each doughnut is titled '<pivot value> - <label>'. Keep labels unique across entries so viewers can tell the doughnuts apart.

settings.title: Settings
settings.description: Configuration options for the doughnut appearance and data processing.

cutout.title: Doughnut Hole Size
cutout.description: How big in percent of the outer radius should the hole in the middle of the doughnut be? From 0% to 90%: set 0% for a pie chart; larger values are capped at 90% so a ring always remains. Unset, blank or not a number uses 50%. Common values: 50% for standard doughnut, 70% for thin ring. The percentages inside the ring get smaller as the ring gets thinner and are hidden when the hole is larger than 75%.

averageLatest.title: Average Latest Values
averageLatest.description: Average each slice over the given number of newest rows instead of drawing only the newest row: each slice becomes the mean of the same slice (matched by position) in those rows. When split by a pivot column, each doughnut averages its own newest rows. Missing, null, blank and non-numeric values are left out of the mean. Unset or below 1 draws the newest row without modification. Useful for smoothing volatile data.

sections.title: Data
sections.description: The slices of this doughnut, as a list of rows of slices. Only the newest row is drawn (or the newest rows averaged, see Average Latest Values). When bound to a table, EACH ROW of the table is one whole doughnut: map one entry per slice, with each value a column of that row and the name usually a constant. The widget never turns rows into slices, so a table with one row per category cannot be shown as shares here: it would draw one 100% slice.

items.title: Sections of the Doughnut
items.description: The slices of one doughnut, i.e. one row of the chosen table. Each item in this array defines a section/slice. Only the newest row is drawn.

name.title: Section Label
name.description: The text shown next to this slice and in its tooltip (the widget has no legend). Should be a chosen constant and usually not be assigned dynamically by a table column value.

value.title: Value
value.description: The numeric value determining the size of this section relative to other sections. Can be bound to a data column for dynamic updates. A slice of 0 takes no space and gets no label; when all slices are 0 or missing, the doughnut shows an empty grey ring.

color.title: Section Color
color.description: The fill color for this doughnut section. Should be a chosen constant and usually not be assigned dynamically by a table column value. Use distinct colors for each section to improve readability.

pivot.title: Split Data by
pivot.description: You can specify a column in the input data to draw a separate doughnut for each distinct value in this column, titled '<value> - <label>'. Bind the SAME column on every slice of the row: each row goes to the doughnut of the first non-empty split value among its slices, and rows without one go to one extra doughnut titled with just the label. The doughnuts are ordered by value, numbers naturally (2 before 10). E.g. with a table [machine, tsp, good_parts, scrap_parts], the slices 'Good' = good_parts and 'Scrap' = scrap_parts, both split by machine, give one Good/Scrap doughnut per machine.
